newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing juror excused from serving.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing juror excused from serving.

text.p: A retired federal government worker was excused Friday from serving on the Oklahoma City bombing trial jury after he said he had colleagues who worked at the federal building that was bombed and did not know if he could be fair.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch said in dismissing the man: "We appreciate your being very honest and we're going to excuse you in this case. It's too much to ask."

The retired Federal Highway Administration employee said he was angry with defendant Timothy McVeigh, who is accused of the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.
"I guess he's been charged, so I guess that anger is there," the unidentified potential juror told the court.
The judge called prosecutors and defence attorneys to a private conference at the bench, which ended with Matsch telling the man that he was being excused.
"This is not anything against you as a person. I'm very sure you've been honest with us and we're going to excuse you in this case," the judge said.

The man was the fifth juror to be publicly dismissed during three weeks of jury selection. Some 89 potential jurors have been questioned so far. The judge has not announced how many have been excused for specific reasons such as total opposition to the death penalty.
Another potential juror needed prompting from the judge Friday before he remembered several run-ins with the law.

"It's coming back to you, is it?" Matsch asked the man who had failed to list on a 40-page questionnaire that he had paid a $50 fine after being charged with reckless endangerment. The man said he remembered the incident after the judge told him he had a computer printout of the record.

The man explained that he simply forgot the 1993 incident, in which his cat jumped on a kitchen table, knocking a .357 handgun to the floor, where it discharged a bullet that ricocheted off a television set and settled inside a wall.

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have been questioning candidates for 15 days to assemble a jury of 12 plus six alternates to decide McVeigh's fate. The Gulf War veteran has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.
A jury is expected to be picked next week, with opening arguments to follow. The trial is expected to last several months.

Prospective jurors are asked a range of questions including whether they or members of their families have had problems with the law in order to gauge attitudes about the criminal justice system. Views on the death penalty also figure prominently in the questioning.

Security remained tight in Denver a day ahead of the bombing anniversary. Barricades circle the downtown Denver city block that houses the federal courthouse and four mounted policemen were posted across the street from the courthouse.
